checks: Compactness of the sampled set gives weak compactness of its probabilities. Every finite ambient convex test is continuous, and the quadratic functional is continuous on the compact support.

Two distinct same-parity support points can be separated in both physical location and their fixed base charts. Coupling equal-mass restrictions and doubling their midpoint law preserves probability and decreases each convex integral. The exact quadratic drop is half the integral of the quadratic of the separation, which is positive.

An integral combination of two or more distinct support bases permits moving proportional positive atomic mass to the physical combination, which remains sampled. Strict Jensen excludes both a nonvertex atom and an extra lattice point of the convex hull.
The positive-atom count is at most 2^n. Restricting a compact physical martingale to a positive atom of mass at least 2^−n gives a second marginal of that mass dominated by the original measure.
Source 0915985a8bcdfd44 §2 states these conclusions for arbitrary probability on the compact sample and arbitrary positive-definite ambient quadratic, with no density or uniformity conclusion.

dependencies.hypotheses: Apply to the compact optimal probability and original compact probability, of the same mass and compared against all finite ambient convex tests. The martingale identity applied to the indicator of a positive source atom gives the barycenter of the restricted second marginal.

overlap.comparison: The finite base allocation in its proof has the same merging argument and produces a lattice-empty vertex hull for ordinary intrinsic mixed volume. Its base quadratic and convex-cell realization do not assert that every minimizer for an arbitrary physical measure and positive-definite full-space quadratic has this property.

readability: The atom has a dominated source submeasure of its own mass, with no geometric density claim for that submeasure.
review_method: Independent mathematical proof review of the frozen normalized candidate
summary: Every minimizing law satisfies the parity and empty-hull constraints. The large atom represents a submeasure of the original physical law.
